newsitem.title: USA: Clinton goes to Congress for budget talks.
newsitem.headline: Clinton goes to Congress for budget talks.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Tuesday kicked off discussions with bipartisan congressional leaders on his balanced budget plan and other key issues with the prediction that they could "do great things together."
Reflecting the new will to promote bipartisanship, Republican leaders invited Clinton to visit them on Capitol Hill for talks on budget, taxes and other subjects.
Just before he left for the meeting with Republican and Democratic leaders of the Senate and House of Representatives, Clinton said he was optimistic about prospects for eventual agreement.
"I think we have got an enormous opportunity here to do great things together," he told reporters during a White House meeting on campaign finance reform.
"The whole system is kind of tending toward movement, instead of paralysis, again and that's a good thing for America. I want to do what I can to keep it going this morning."

The invitation represented a sea change for Republicans. Last year they tried to force the White House to accept their conservative agenda and then found the public blamed them, not Clinton, for the unpopular government shutdowns that ensued.
Now, they too say they are optimistic about the chances of reaching an early deal to balance the budget by the year 2002 and are eager to talk.

All sides -- the White House, the Republicans who control Congress and Clinton's own minority Democrats -- carefully avoided labeling Tuesday's meeting a budget negotiation, saying it is too early for the give-and-take of a formal bargaining session.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry cautioned reporters: "This is not commencement of a budget negotiation," and noted that other issues will be discussed.
"It's too early for negotiations with the president on the budget," Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle of South Dakota concurred.

Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott of Mississippi emphasised that in addition to discussions on balancing the budget and cutting taxes, topics will include education, crime and drugs and the environment as the five parts of "the critical agenda facing our country."

None of the House or Senate budget committee leaders were invited to attend. And Congress plans to carry on with the routine series of hearings on Clinton's budget with numerous Cabinet officials testifying this week.
Clinton last week presented his new budget, winning a cool reception from Republicans.

But they said it would be the starting point for talks on spending and taxes. Senate Budget Committee chairman Pete Domenici said it was "alive on arrival," unlike last year's plan, which was trashed before entering the Capitol doors.

The New Mexico Republican and many others in his party expressed reservations about Clinton's delayed spending cuts, criticised the proposed $98 billion tax cut as too small and said it lacked the major steps needed to save the Medicare health care programme for the elderly.

Whether Republicans come up with a separate attempt to balance the budget by the year 2000 remains to be decided. House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Bill Archer, a Texas Republican, said they will decide after they have seen how much progress is made in the budget committees.

"I think a lot of Americans, including all the Republicans, I think, here in Congress, share his values ... Where we disagree, is how to get there," House Republican Conference Chairman John Boehner said on Fox News Sunday.

The president's proposal, unveiled Feb. 6, envisions the government's budget being brought into balance by 2002 and remaining there for the next 10 to 20 years, a sharp contrast with the past 26 years of rising red ink in Washington.

To get there, some of the headway made against the deficit in the last four years would be lost. Clinton's plan would not produce a deficit below 1996's $107 billion until the year 2000. It would add spending for education and welfare and give families a $98 billion tax cut over the five years. And it would raise other taxes by $76 billion and reduce Medicare.
